references.text: At the institution of the Lord's Supper, Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it and gave it to the disciples – exactly the same sequence of actions as in the meal at Emmaus ([ref:Luk 22:19|Luke 22:19]).

At the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus took the loaves, blessed them, broke them and gave them to the disciples – the same characteristic pattern of taking, blessing, breaking and giving ([ref:Matt 14:19|Matthew 14:19]).
Also at the feeding of the four thousand, Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, broke them and gave them to the disciples, reflecting the same liturgical action ([ref:Matt 15:36|Matthew 15:36]).

Matthew's account of the Lord's Supper uses the same pattern: Jesus took bread, blessed it, broke it and gave it to the disciples – a pattern that was recognizable to the travelers on the road to Emmaus ([ref:Matt 26:26|Matthew 26:26]).
Mark's account of the feeding of the five thousand contains the same sequence: Jesus took the loaves, blessed them, broke them and gave them to the disciples ([ref:Mark 6:41|Mark 6:41]).
Mark's account of the Lord's Supper shows the same action where Jesus takes bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it – the Eucharistic action that characterized Jesus ([ref:Mark 14:22|Mark 14:22]).
Paul links the breaking of bread to fellowship with the body of Christ, showing that the early church recognized Christ precisely in the breaking of bread ([ref:1 Kor 10:16|1 Corinthians 10:16]).
The first church held fast to the breaking of bread as a central part of their worship – a practice rooted in scenes such as the meal at Emmaus ([ref:Apg 2:42|Acts 2:42]).
The believers broke bread in their homes and ate together with gladness – a continuation of fellowship with the risen Christ in the breaking of bread ([ref:Apg 2:46|Acts 2:46]).

Shortly after this verse, the travelers on the road to Emmaus report that they recognized Jesus precisely when he broke the bread – the breaking of bread became the decisive moment of recognition ([ref:Luk 24:35|Luke 24:35]).
Luke's own account of the feeding of the five thousand uses the same fourfold action: took, blessed, broke and gave – a pattern that points forward to Emmaus ([ref:Luk 9:16|Luke 9:16]).
